decision.explanation: The vertex (0,-7) gives a=7. For a vertical hyperbola, asymptotes have slopes ±a/b, so 7/b=7/6 gives b=6. Thus y²/49−x²/36=1, parametrized by x=6 tan(t), y=7 sec(t), since sec²(t)−tan²(t)=1.

Find the parametric equations of the hyperbola shown above given that its asymptotes are $y=\pm \frac{7}{6}x.$
after.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a vertical hyperbola centered at the origin with Cartesian equation

$$
\frac{{y}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1
$$

are given by 

$$
x=b\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,y=a\operatorname{sec}⁡t,
$$

where $a$ and $b$ are positive constants.

The vertices of the hyperbola occur at $(0,\pm a).$ From the graph, we have that $(0,-7)$ is a vertex of the hyperbola, so $a=7.$

Recall also that the asymptotes of the hyperbola occur at $y=\pm \frac{a}{b}x.$ In our case, the asymptotes are

$$
y=\pm \frac{7}{6}x.
$$

Equating the coefficients of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{a}{b} & =\frac{7}{6} \\ \frac{7}{b} & =\frac{7}{6} \\ b & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the hyperbola are

$$
x=6\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,y=7\operatorname{sec}⁡t.
$$

Find the parametric equations of the hyperbola shown above given that its asymptotes are y=±76x.

a
 x=9tan⁡t,y=7sec⁡t
b
 x=9sec⁡t,y=7tan⁡t
c
 x=6tan⁡t,y=7sec⁡t
d
 x=7tan⁡t,y=6sec⁡t
e
 x=7sec⁡t,y=6tan⁡t
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The parametric equations of a vertical hyperbola centered at the origin with Cartesian equation y2a2−x2b2=1

are given by x=btan⁡t,y=asec⁡t,

where a and b are positive constants.

The vertices of the hyperbola occur at (0,±a). From the graph, we have that (0,−7) is a vertex of the hyperbola, so a=7.

Recall also that the asymptotes of the hyperbola occur at y=±abx. In our case, the asymptotes are y=±76x.

Equating the coefficients of x, we get ab=767b=76b=6.

Therefore, the parametric equations of the hyperbola are x=6tan⁡t,y=7sec⁡t.

content.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a vertical hyperbola centered at the origin with Cartesian equation

$$
\frac{{y}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1
$$

are given by 

$$
x=b\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,y=a\operatorname{sec}⁡t,
$$

where $a$ and $b$ are positive constants.

The vertices of the hyperbola occur at $(0,\pm a).$ From the graph, we have that $(0,-7)$ is a vertex of the hyperbola, so $a=7.$

Recall also that the asymptotes of the hyperbola occur at $y=\pm \frac{a}{b}x.$ In our case, the asymptotes are

$$
y=\pm \frac{7}{6}x.
$$

Equating the coefficients of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{a}{b} & =\frac{7}{6} \\ \frac{7}{b} & =\frac{7}{6} \\ b & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the hyperbola are

$$
x=6\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,y=7\operatorname{sec}⁡t.
$$

decision.explanation: The vertex (0,-1) gives a=1. The asymptote slopes ±a/b=±1 give b=1. Therefore the hyperbola is y²−x²=1, parametrized by x=tan(t), y=sec(t) using sec²(t)−tan²(t)=1.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14068362/assets/245037d572c2bc9c81d3cdfb7a485b167c15223c68e3dbb8e40eaa2cc7650da9.png)

Find the parametric equations of the hyperbola shown above given that its asymptotes are $y=\pm x.$
after.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a vertical hyperbola centered at the origin with Cartesian equation

$$
\frac{{y}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1
$$

are given by 

$$
x=b\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,y=a\operatorname{sec}⁡t,
$$

where $a$ and $b$ are positive constants.

The vertices of the hyperbola occur at $(0,\pm a).$ From the graph, we have that $(0,-1)$ is a vertex of the hyperbola, so $a=1.$

Recall also that the asymptotes of the hyperbola occur at $y=\pm \frac{a}{b}x.$ In our case, the asymptotes are

$$
y=\pm x.
$$

Equating the coefficients of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{a}{b} & =1 \\ \frac{1}{b} & =1 \\ b & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the hyperbola are

$$
x=\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,y=\operatorname{sec}⁡t.
$$

Question 2
?

Find the parametric equations of the hyperbola shown above given that its asymptotes are y=±x.

a
x=tan⁡t,y=2sec⁡t
b
x=tan⁡t,y=sec⁡t
c
x=2tan⁡t,y=2sec⁡t
d
x=sec⁡t,y=tan⁡t
e
x=2sec⁡t,y=2tan⁡t
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The parametric equations of a vertical hyperbola centered at the origin with Cartesian equation y2a2−x2b2=1

are given by x=btan⁡t,y=asec⁡t,

where a and b are positive constants.

The vertices of the hyperbola occur at (0,±a). From the graph, we have that (0,−1) is a vertex of the hyperbola, so a=1.

Recall also that the asymptotes of the hyperbola occur at y=±abx. In our case, the asymptotes are y=±x.

Equating the coefficients of x, we get ab=11b=1b=1.

Therefore, the parametric equations of the hyperbola are x=tan⁡t,y=sec⁡t.

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms a=b=1, so x=tan(t), y=sec(t) satisfies y²−x²=1 and has the given vertices and asymptotes. Option d instead satisfies x²−y²=1, a horizontal hyperbola; its deliberately incorrect submission does not contradict the earlier answer b.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14068362/assets/245037d572c2bc9c81d3cdfb7a485b167c15223c68e3dbb8e40eaa2cc7650da9.png)

Find the parametric equations of the hyperbola shown above given that its asymptotes are $y=\pm x.$
content.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a vertical hyperbola centered at the origin with Cartesian equation

$$
\frac{{y}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1
$$

are given by 

$$
x=b\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,y=a\operatorname{sec}⁡t,
$$

where $a$ and $b$ are positive constants.

The vertices of the hyperbola occur at $(0,\pm a).$ From the graph, we have that $(0,-1)$ is a vertex of the hyperbola, so $a=1.$

Recall also that the asymptotes of the hyperbola occur at $y=\pm \frac{a}{b}x.$ In our case, the asymptotes are

$$
y=\pm x.
$$

Equating the coefficients of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{a}{b} & =1 \\ \frac{1}{b} & =1 \\ b & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the hyperbola are

$$
x=\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,y=\operatorname{sec}⁡t.
$$

after.name: Question 3
after.problem: Find the Cartesian equation of the hyperbola $x=\sqrt{5}\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,y=3\operatorname{sec}⁡t.$
after.worked_solution:
To find the Cartesian equation of the hyperbola, we need to eliminate the parameter $t.$ We can do this using the secant-tangent Identity.

- Isolating the $\operatorname{tan}⁡t$ term in the $x$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\sqrt{5}\operatorname{tan}⁡t \\ \frac{x}{\sqrt{5}} & =\operatorname{tan}⁡t \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{(\sqrt{5})^{2}} & ={tan}^{2}⁡t \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{5} & ={tan}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

- Isolating the $\operatorname{sec}⁡t$ term in the $y$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =3\operatorname{sec}⁡t \\ \frac{y}{3} & =\operatorname{sec}⁡t \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{{3}^{2}} & ={sec}^{2}⁡t \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{9} & ={sec}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the two equations into the identity ${tan}^{2}⁡t+1={sec}^{2}⁡t$ and rearranging, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{tan}^{2}⁡t+1 & ={sec}^{2}⁡t \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{5}+1 & =\frac{{y}^{2}}{9} \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{9}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{5} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

content.problem: Find the Cartesian equation of the hyperbola $x=\sqrt{5}\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,y=3\operatorname{sec}⁡t.$
content.worked_solution:
To find the Cartesian equation of the hyperbola, we need to eliminate the parameter $t.$ We can do this using the secant-tangent Identity.

- Isolating the $\operatorname{tan}⁡t$ term in the $x$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\sqrt{5}\operatorname{tan}⁡t \\ \frac{x}{\sqrt{5}} & =\operatorname{tan}⁡t \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{(\sqrt{5})^{2}} & ={tan}^{2}⁡t \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{5} & ={tan}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

- Isolating the $\operatorname{sec}⁡t$ term in the $y$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =3\operatorname{sec}⁡t \\ \frac{y}{3} & =\operatorname{sec}⁡t \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{{3}^{2}} & ={sec}^{2}⁡t \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{9} & ={sec}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the two equations into the identity ${tan}^{2}⁡t+1={sec}^{2}⁡t$ and rearranging, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{tan}^{2}⁡t+1 & ={sec}^{2}⁡t \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{5}+1 & =\frac{{y}^{2}}{9} \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{9}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{5} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 4
?

One branch of a hyperbola (shown above) is defined by the parametric equations

x=3tan⁡t,y=6sec⁡t.

What is the domain of the parameter t?

a
t∈[−π,π],t≠0
b
t∈(−π2,π2)
c
t∈[−π,π],t≠±π2
d
t∈[−π,−π2)∪(π2,π]
e
t∈[0,π],t≠π2
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The parametric equations of the full hyperbola are

x=3tan⁡t,y=6sec⁡t,t∈[−π,π],t≠±π2.

To restrict the parameterization to a single branch, we refer to the diagram below.

We can see that if we restrict t to (−π2,π2), we get only the upper branch.

Therefore, the parametric equations that describe only the upper branch are

x=3tan⁡t,y=6sec⁡t,t∈(−π2,π2).

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms option b. On (−π/2,π/2), sec(t)>0 and tan(t) ranges over all real numbers, tracing exactly the upper branch. Option c also includes negative sec(t), tracing the lower branch as well.

$$
x=3\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,y=6\operatorname{sec}⁡t,\,t\in (-\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2}).
$$

Question 5
?

One branch of a hyperbola (shown above) is defined by the parametric equations

x=5tan⁡t,y=13sec⁡t.

What is the domain of the parameter t?

a
t∈[−π,π],t≠±π2
b
t∈[−π,π],t≠0
c
t∈[0,π],t≠π2
d
t∈(−π2,π2)
e
t∈[−π,−π2)∪(π2,π]
Submit

decision.explanation: The upper branch requires y=(1/3)sec(t)>0. On (−π/2,π/2), cos(t)>0 and x=5tan(t) ranges from −∞ to ∞, tracing exactly the entire upper branch. The endpoints are excluded because tan(t) and sec(t) are undefined there.

after.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14068362/assets/1474fb8efcada2aec61c1aa2b2ed16615e0ba968ec4e53a8fbfe05b1107c085f.png)

One branch of a hyperbola (shown above) is defined by the parametric equations

$$
x=5\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,y=\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sec}⁡t.
$$

What is the domain of the parameter $t?$
after.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of the full hyperbola are

$$
x=5\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,y=\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sec}⁡t,\,t\in [-\pi ,\pi ],\,t\ne \pm \frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

To restrict the parameterization to a single branch, we refer to the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14068362/assets/46c9d9139a3cff2a76871c69deeac60492d2c9aef4bf1f7ac07a16868d31d6e0.png)

We can see that if we restrict $t$ to $(-\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2}),$ we get only the upper branch.

Therefore, the parametric equations that describe only the upper branch are

$$
x=5\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,y=\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sec}⁡t,\,t\in (-\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2}).
$$

Question 5

One branch of a hyperbola (shown above) is defined by the parametric equations

x=5tan⁡t,y=13sec⁡t.

What is the domain of the parameter t?

a
t∈[−π,π],t≠±π2
b
t∈[−π,π],t≠0
c
t∈[0,π],t≠π2
d
t∈(−π2,π2)
e
t∈[−π,−π2)∪(π2,π]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The parametric equations of the full hyperbola are

x=5tan⁡t,y=13sec⁡t,t∈[−π,π],t≠±π2.

To restrict the parameterization to a single branch, we refer to the diagram below.

We can see that if we restrict t to (−π2,π2), we get only the upper branch.

Therefore, the parametric equations that describe only the upper branch are

x=5tan⁡t,y=13sec⁡t,t∈(−π2,π2).

One branch of a hyperbola (shown above) is defined by the parametric equations

$$
x=5\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,y=\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sec}⁡t.
$$

What is the domain of the parameter $t?$
content.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of the full hyperbola are

$$
x=5\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,y=\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sec}⁡t,\,t\in [-\pi ,\pi ],\,t\ne \pm \frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

To restrict the parameterization to a single branch, we refer to the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14068362/assets/46c9d9139a3cff2a76871c69deeac60492d2c9aef4bf1f7ac07a16868d31d6e0.png)

We can see that if we restrict $t$ to $(-\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2}),$ we get only the upper branch.

Therefore, the parametric equations that describe only the upper branch are

$$
x=5\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,y=\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sec}⁡t,\,t\in (-\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2}).
$$
